title: Jesus's prayer at the supper (CCC 2746–2751)
hookLine: John 17, the prayer of the hour
tomorrow: The whole gospel in a prayer

cards: The supper is over. The feet have been washed. Judas has gone out into the night.
For chapters, John's Gospel has let Jesus talk to his friends at the table: about a vine and its branches, a helper who will come, a sorrow that will turn to joy.
Then, with the garden and the arrest a short walk away, he stops talking to them. He lifts his eyes and talks to his Father, out loud, with them still in the room. They get to overhear it.
So do we. Today: Jesus's prayer at the supper.

teach.b: John 17 opens, in the Douay-Rheims: "Father, the hour is come, glorify thy Son, that thy Son may glorify thee." Earlier in John, his hour had not yet come. Now it has.

The Catechism calls this the prayer of the hour of Jesus, and says Christian tradition rightly names it his priestly prayer: a high priest praying on the edge of offering himself. It moves outward in rings.
First he prays for himself, to finish the work he was given.

Then for the friends in the room, and here's the line that surprises: "I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil." Not their escape. Kept, right where they are.

Then the ring widens past the room and past that night: "And not for them only do I pray, but for them also who through their word shall believe in me." Catholics hear every later believer in that line, down to today.

teach.h: THAT THEY ALL MAY BE ONE.
teach.b: And what he asks for them is "That they all may be one." The Catechism adds that this prayer, like his sacrifice, reaches to the end of time.
And the Our Father's requests are already folded in: the Father's name, his work finished, his people kept from evil. In the Catholic reading, the prayer he taught and the prayer he prayed are one.

how: Catholics hear John 17 read at Mass in the weeks of Easter, and its words "that they all may be one" are sometimes used at gatherings for Christian unity.

games.q: the supper is over, Judas has gone out, and Jesus is praying aloud for his friends. what does he ask the Father to do with them?
o: take them out of the world, to safety.
keep them from evil, right where they are.
make them powerful against their enemies.
games.why: "I pray not that thou shouldst take them out of the world, but that thou shouldst keep them from evil." not escape: being kept.

practice: If you have a Bible or a phone nearby, read John chapter seventeen slowly, as far as you get; if not, hold one line: "That they all may be one." Notice who's in each ring: himself, his friends, people not yet born.
If you pray, let yourself be one of the ones he prays for; if you don't, just stay with what he asks.

wordCard.voice: Jesus's prayer at the supper. John 17, which the Catechism calls the prayer of the hour, his priestly prayer for his friends and for all who would believe through them.
